Senses.PreferredTarget: open the way and let the encounter proceed
AlternateTargets: let pass rather than hold fast
give the other side room to move
Senses.Explanation: In a public encounter, to open the way and allow movement instead of blocking or holding fast. The recurrent contrast is with “hold fast” or “hold in place,” and the records make the difference visible through their own images. Tianzhang Yuanshan says that holding fast freezes dripping water and stops the rivers, while releasing brings warm sun, mild wind, and mountains and streams competing in beauty; he then asks which is good. Xuedou Chongxian says that under release rubble shines, while under restraint true gold loses color. Yinyuan Longqi opens a cloth bag, opens one road of release, and lets the assembly jump east and west before asking which is release and which is restraint. Tiantong Hongjue Min is asked for “a releasing saying” after the restraining side is set aside; he answers, “open in all directions.” Yuanwu Keqin asks whether releasing for people or holding them fast is good. Wumen Huikai says that holding fast and releasing each puts out one hand to raise the ancestral vehicle. Yongjue Yuanxian contrasts Boshan Wuyi, who only knew how to hold fast, with his own release on that day. The phrase has 1,169 occurrences in 247 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: To let pass is to refrain from stopping, striking, exposing, or penalizing someone or something that could have been checked. Chan comments use the ordinary act of letting something pass to judge a missed intervention or a deliberately conceded move; those stances do not create different lexical senses.

Senses.Explanation: The many blind people feeling an elephant each encounter a part and mistake partial contact for the whole animal. Xiangtian Jinian explicitly reads the elephant comparison as exposing the illness of clinging to one's own view. Dahui Zonggao lists it among cases that must be met personally rather than settled in speech. Xutang Zhiyu says the blind know an elephant yet do not see the whole; an unnamed questioner asks Zhaozhou what the true elephant is when each gives a different account, and Zhaozhou answers that there is no reliance—one simply does not know. The Chan bend turns the comparison into a public test of whether partial descriptions are being promoted as complete seeing.
